solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Each article is penned by idiotic fool

indicators.note: something penned is shut inside a pen

parts.note: mad = idiotic; it opens around the next two pieces
ea. is the abbreviation for each, as on a price list

explanation.surface: A sneer at a newspaper whose every piece is written by an idiot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Article' sits in a newspaper picture, so it reads as a piece of writing rather than the grammar word THE.
explanation.definitionFit: A meathead is a slang word for a stupid person, a fool.

clue.text: Test for car drivers repeatedly exposed reason to act

indicators.note: exposing a word strips its outer letters; doing it twice takes two layers off each end

parts.note: the MOT is the annual roadworthiness test for cars in Britain
DRIVERS loses D and S, then R and R, leaving IVE

explanation.surface: A driving test that keeps catching out learners gives them a reason to do something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Test for car drivers' looks like the driving test, but the break falls after 'car': the MOT is Britain's yearly check of a car's roadworthiness.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a motive is literally what moves a person, from the Latin movere.

clue.text: Tackle a quiet matter — getting a rodent caught

parts.note: pus is the matter in a wound; it wraps around A RAT

explanation.surface: Someone quietly dealing with an awkward business in which a rat has been trapped.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tackle' reads as a verb, to deal with a matter, but it is the noun: gear, as in fishing tackle.
explanation.definitionFit: Tackle is equipment, and apparatus is equipment for a job.

clue.text: Is male pursuing the female's love an act of gallantry?

definitions.note: strictly, heroism is the quality shown in an act of gallantry

parts.note: love = zero in tennis scoring, the letter O

explanation.surface: A question whether a man chasing a woman's love counts as gallant behaviour.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a courtship, so 'love' feels like romance; here it is the tennis nil.
explanation.definitionFit: Heroism is brave, gallant conduct, the stuff of an act of gallantry.

clue.text: Disuse opiates for treating fatty lumps?

indicators.note: the letters of DISUSE OPIATES are processed, worked into a new shape

explanation.surface: Advice to give up painkillers when dealing with lumps of fat.
explanation.walkthrough: The medical surface makes 'treating' look like a doctor's word, which is why the anagram hides. The question mark admits that fatty lumps is a loose description.
explanation.definitionFit: Adipose tissue is the body's fat, which can gather in fatty lumps.

clue.text: Writer's means of conveying part of her writing

parts.note: the writer speaks of themself: writer's = writer is = I AM

explanation.surface: A writer's way of getting across a piece of her work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Writer's' is not possessive: it is writer is, and the writer of a clue calls themself I, so I AM. The definition makes the same writer a poet whose lines use this metrical foot.
explanation.definitionFit: An iambus, or iamb, is a metrical foot, one of the units a poet's writing is built from.

clue.text: Beautiful female song with death coming up

parts.note: an aria is an operatic song

indicators.note: in a down entry, coming up means reading from bottom to top

parts.note: death = the end; it is turned over to DNE

explanation.surface: A lovely woman singing while death draws near, like an operatic heroine.
explanation.walkthrough: Ariadne is the princess of Greek myth who gave Theseus the thread through the labyrinth; the opera surface points at Strauss's Ariadne auf Naxos.
explanation.definitionFit: Ariadne, the Cretan princess of myth, is a beautiful female figure.

clue.text: Shout, getting neighbour ultimately in quarrel

indicators.note: the ultimate letter is the last one
'in' places one thing inside another, so neighbour's last letter sits inside the shout

explanation.surface: Shouting erupts when a neighbour finally gets drawn into a row.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads straight through as a garden-fence dispute, so 'in quarrel' looks like wordplay; only 'quarrel' is the definition and 'in' is the container.
explanation.definitionFit: A near synonym, though a brawl is a quarrel that has turned rowdy and physical.

clue.text: Daily, set out in dependable manner

indicators.note: out = in disarray, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A cleaner, a daily, sets out to do the job reliably.
explanation.walkthrough: A daily is British for a cleaner who comes in each day, so the surface is about domestic help; the comma stops you reading 'set out' as one verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a steady worker is a dependable one, and the adverb follows.

clue.text: Gradually decrease source of light

definitions.meaning: a verb: to narrow or dwindle bit by bit, as a spire does
a noun: a thin candle or waxed wick used to light others

explanation.surface: An instruction to dim the lights slowly.
explanation.walkthrough: The two halves run together as one instruction about dimming a lamp; split them and TAPER answers each, first as a verb, then as the slender candle.
explanation.definitionFit: A taper narrows gradually, and a taper is also a slender candle.

clue.text: One helper carries most of building material — overlapping like tiles

indicators.note: most of a word is all but its last letter

parts.note: a mate is an assistant, as in a plumber's mate; it opens around BRIC

explanation.surface: A builder's labourer hauling most of the bricks, on a roofing job.
explanation.walkthrough: IMBRICATE is a rare adjective from Latin imbrex, a roof tile; the building surface is apt, which helps a solver who has never met the word.
explanation.definitionFit: Imbricate describes things laid so that they overlap like roof tiles or fish scales.

clue.text: After ban on profit, watch someone looking for good deal

parts.note: a hunter is a pocket watch with a hinged lid over its face

explanation.surface: A ban on profiteering is followed by keeping an eye on anyone after a cheap deal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Watch' reads as a verb, to keep an eye on, but it is the noun: a hunter is a pocket watch with a protective cover.
explanation.definitionFit: A bargain hunter is someone who shops around for a good deal.

clue.text: Unwelcome feeling, having risen to great heights?

definitions.text: Unwelcome feeling, having risen to great heights?

parts.note: the surface suggests envy or smugness at someone's success; the setter means a physical sensation
read as a career triumph, but taken literally it is being high up and looking down

explanation.surface: Success going to someone's head, an ambitious climber's unease.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Risen to great heights' sounds like a career triumph; read literally, it is someone up a tall building feeling dizzy.
explanation.definitionFit: Vertigo is the unwelcome giddy feeling people get when high up.

clue.text: King confused and showing signs of age?

explanation.surface: An old monarch growing muddled and worn with the years.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface paints an ageing king, so 'confused' seems part of the description of age; it is wordplay, and only the last phrase defines.
explanation.definitionFit: Raddled means worn and haggard, showing the ravages of age or hard living.

clue.text: Excitable soldiers chat endlessly, backing an agent encountered retreating

indicators.note: TALK loses its last letter
MENTAL backs up the rest, standing behind it
an army retreating goes back the way it came, so these letters run right to left

parts.note: a rep is a sales agent, a representative
men = soldiers, as opposed to officers

explanation.surface: Jumpy troops chattering while a secret agent they met pulls back.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue gives the back half first: MENTAL is 'backing' TEMPERA, standing behind it, so the pieces read in the opposite order to the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: someone at the mercy of their temperament is easily excited and moody.

clue.text: Generous guest and host with no end of charm somewhere in Ireland

indicators.note: 'with no' means lacking, so the host must do without the letter that follows

parts.note: a guest who tips generously is a tipper

indicators.note: the end of charm is its last letter, M

parts.words: host with no end of charm
parts.note: host = ARMY, a great multitude; it loses M, the last letter of charM

explanation.surface: A lavish guest and an unfailingly charming host, somewhere in Irish hospitality.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Host' pairs with 'guest' to look like hospitality, but it is the old sense of an army; and 'no end of charm' reads as 'plenty of charm'.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: Tipperary is a county and town in Ireland, famous from the wartime song about the long way there.

clue.text: Indicate new element in one sort of table

definitions.text: element in one sort of table

indicators.note: INDICATE made new, rebuilt in another order

explanation.surface: An instruction to mark a newly found element on a table.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One sort of table' is the periodic table, not a dining table or a chart of figures; the surface's talk of new elements makes it sound like a chemistry lesson, which it half is.
explanation.definitionFit: An actinide is any of the fifteen radioactive metals from actinium to lawrencium in the periodic table.

clue.text: Steward's office surprisingly unsophisticated, needing time and energy to be spent

indicators.note: surprisingly signals the letters come out in an unexpected order

parts.note: anagram fodder, 15 letters before the deletion

explanation.surface: A steward's post turns out to be unexpectedly crude, eating up time and effort.
explanation.walkthrough: UNSOPHISTICATED has one T too many and an E too many; take one of each out and the remaining 13 letters rearrange to the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Custodianship is the office or role of a custodian, a steward in charge of something.

clue.text: Wild animals, many buried under old church

explanation.surface: A graveyard where wild creatures lie buried in numbers under an ancient church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Buried' suggests one thing hidden inside another, but in a down clue it only places LOTS below the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by class: the ocelot is a spotted wild cat of the Americas, one kind of wild animal.

clue.text: Climber's goal? Hard work involving bad track initially

indicators.note: the initial letter of track

parts.note: op = opus, a work; H and OP enclose ILL T

explanation.surface: A mountaineer's aim reached by a hard slog along a poor path.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hard work' reads as one phrase for a slog, but it splits into two abbreviations that together form the outer shell.
explanation.definitionFit: The top of a hill is a climber's goal, though a modest one, hence the question mark.

clue.text: Bird entering school is a bit of a pain

parts.note: sch. is the abbreviation for school; it opens around TIT
a tit is a small songbird

explanation.surface: A bird that gets into a school is a nuisance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A bit of a pain' sounds like mild annoyance, but it is literal: a stitch is a sharp pain in the side.
explanation.definitionFit: A stitch is a sudden sharp pain in the side, so a bit of pain.

clue.text: Possibly cold current associated with three lochs

definitions.note: 'Possibly cold' defines by example: a cold is possibly an illness

parts.note: I is the symbol for electric current
L and L, the map abbreviation for loch, then Loch NESS by name

explanation.surface: A chilly stream that feeds three Scottish lakes.
explanation.walkthrough: A loch is a Scottish lake; two are given as L, and the third is the most famous of all, Ness. 'Cold' is the illness, not the temperature of the water.
explanation.definitionFit: A cold is one example of an illness, as 'possibly' signals.

clue.text: River left with organic compound, river being destroyed

indicators.note: the R for river is wiped out of ETHER

parts.note: ETHER, an organic compound, without R for river

explanation.surface: A river spoilt by chemical waste, one river after another ruined.
explanation.walkthrough: The Lethe is the river of forgetfulness in the Greek underworld. 'River' appears twice: once as the definition, once as the R to be removed.
explanation.definitionFit: Lethe is a river of Hades in Greek myth, whose water made the dead forget.

clue.text: University student finally penning grand stories, most foul

indicators.note: the final letter of student

parts.note: g = grand, a thousand pounds or dollars
lies = stories, as a child tells stories

explanation.surface: A university student at last writing grand tales of the most unpleasant kind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'University student' reads as one phrase for an undergraduate, but it splits: U, then the final letter of 'student'.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: foul and ugly both describe the nasty, and the superlatives match.

clue.text: Home and dry, wanderer having got inside perhaps a loner?

definitions.note: defined by example: a loner is perhaps an introvert

indicators.note: the wanderer has got inside, entered, the dry piece, so it sits within it

parts.note: TT = teetotal, a drinker who is dry; it opens around ROVER

explanation.surface: A wanderer finally home and safe, maybe a solitary sort.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Home and dry' is a British idiom for safely finished, but it splits in two; TT, teetotal, is the crossword's usual 'dry'. 'Perhaps' shows a loner is only one kind of introvert.
explanation.definitionFit: An introvert is inward-looking and may well be a loner.

clue.text: Area of land not entirely unattractive

indicators.note: only part of unattractive is used

explanation.surface: A plot of land that is less than lovely.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not entirely unattractive' reads as faint praise, rather pleasant, when it is telling you to take just part of the word.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: tract is the formal word for an expanse of land, as in a tract of forest.

clue.text: Church service has lost two final elements, however

indicators.note: the last two letters, N and G, are dropped

parts.words: Church service has lost two final elements
parts.note: EVENSONG, the evening service, without NG

explanation.surface: A church service cut short of its closing parts.
explanation.walkthrough: Evensong is the Anglican evening service; 'elements' reads as parts of the liturgy but means letters.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: 'even so' concedes a point and carries on regardless, the same job 'however' does.

clue.text: Journey finishes off at lovely church altarpiece?

definitions.note: defined by example: an altarpiece is often a triptych

indicators.note: the finishes of at and lovely are their last letters

parts.note: the last letters of aT and lovelY

explanation.surface: A trip that ends at a lovely church, where the altarpiece awaits.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits a triptych need not be an altarpiece, though many are: three hinged painted panels behind an altar.
explanation.definitionFit: A triptych is a three-panelled painting, often an altarpiece.
